beats.trigger: ## Multi-Agent Systems
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The filesystem is the meeting room.
beats.got: Agents work together by leaving files for each other, though I'm not sure yet what that means in practice.

beats.trigger: [Schedule your personal agent](exercises/personal-agent-homework.md) to read your challenge memory for a week.
beats.got: There was homework I hadn't known about, and it's three links.

beats.trigger: **Analyze** handoff failures: hidden conflicts, clashing dialects, beige averaging
beats.got: The goals are build, analyze and decide when to split. I don't know most of these words yet, 'dialect' and 'beige averaging' in particular.

beats.trigger: Three agents search Confluence, OneDrive and practitioner articles, and three more decide what it means.
beats.got: Some agents fetch material and others judge it. That sounds a bit like how my HR partners and I work.

beats.trigger: Writing a file changes your folder. Slack changes another system.
beats.got: There's a real line between an agent writing a draft and one that acts. The approval step is what keeps a person in the loop, and I can take that to my leadership team.

beats.trigger: Push back when the first answer restates the problem.
beats.got: The agent names the one obstacle that matters most, and I have to challenge it when it just repeats my topic back. I liked being told to push back.

beats.trigger: Three retrievers fetch raw material on your challenge into `sources/`; a fourth session curates it into `memory/`.
beats.got: I open four sessions and paste prompts into each. That's a lot of windows for a Tuesday, and nobody has said who in my team would do this.

beats.trigger: Spawn three helpers with different stances on your curated memory.
beats.got: Helpers can argue from different positions and then be forced into one answer. That is close to how a good leadership debate should go. I also noted the line that I can't tell yet whether the answer is right.

beats.trigger: When do you split, and how?
beats.got: There are two ways to split, and this part helps me choose between them.

beats.trigger: Build one agent per recurring workflow: a single `.md` file, guardrailed for that job.
beats.got: One agent for each job that repeats. That maps onto roles and processes in HR, so I can see how it would spread through a team.

beats.trigger: If one agent can produce what you need, use one.
beats.got: Start with one agent and split only when you have to. A cautious message like that builds trust with me.

beats.trigger: A legal-policy agent shouldn't have customer-data access.
beats.got: I split agents when they need different access, speak a different dialect, or should disagree. The access test is my lever for the works council and the DPO.

beats.trigger: More input does not fix a beige answer.
beats.got: More agents doesn't make the work more careful. It only adds cost and noise.

beats.trigger: The synthesizer then commits to one diagnosis and drops what does not serve it.
beats.got: Give the combining agent a framework and it chooses a position, where otherwise it averages. 'Drops what does not serve it' makes me ask who decides what gets dropped.

beats.trigger: Could one prompt produce the same quality of output?
beats.got: There's a simple test to ask before building anything bigger. I'd use it on vendors who pitch me agent teams.

beats.trigger: **Helper agents in one session (the Phase 2 move).** Pick this for quick parallel thinking with a bounded return.
beats.got: There are separate sessions and helpers inside one session. I only half follow the difference, and it feels like a tool detail.

beats.trigger: Different tools: sessions. Shared tools: helper agents.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Splitting creates handoffs, and handoffs are where work goes wrong.
beats.got: Mistakes happen where one agent hands work to the next, like two numbers where only one survives. It's the same as handovers between people in my org.

beats.trigger: If one well-prompted agent does the job, write that prompt.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Agents get stuck: wrong source, three views averaged into mush, the wrong file written, confident right before a failed handoff.
beats.got: Agents fail in recognisable ways, and this part names them.

beats.trigger: Prompt your stuck system to diagnose whether the bug lives in the sources, the processing, or the boundary between agents.
beats.got: You ask the agent where the fault is before you fix anything. I like that order.

beats.trigger: Write down the lesson: add a rule to CLAUDE.md
beats.got: Each failure gets sorted into sources, processing or boundary, and the lesson goes into a rules file so it spreads to the next person. That's how a habit moves from one person to a team.

beats.trigger: The agent reviews the four prompts, the retrieval files, the synthesizer's briefing and the conversation, then rewrites CLAUDE.md in place and reports what changed.
beats.got: The agent reviews its own session and rewrites the rules file. The step is fine, but it's another technical task with no word about people.

beats.trigger: It does not check whether the briefing is true.
beats.got: The audit looks at handoffs and not at truth. That's honest, and it's the question I'd want to take to leadership.

beats.trigger: Push back where the summary is wrong
beats.got: I'm the one who corrects the agent's account of what went wrong.

beats.trigger: The synthesized briefing's correctness stays an open question today.
beats.got: I leave with an answer I can't verify, and the course says that's fine. That feels honest but uncomfortable.

beats.trigger: **Optional move: pressure-test the memory.**
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Split only where agents can't be one: access, dialect, stance.
beats.got: The summary gives me a short rule to remember: sessions or helpers, and three reasons to split.

beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Agents add non-deterministic behaviour, prompt injection (direct, or inside retrieved text) and emergent capability you can only bound.
beats.got: Agent risk sits on top of normal security. The words are heavy, but I understand that this is where the works council and the DPO come in.

beats.trigger: An agent that works across connected systems has access to those systems.
beats.got: Before I connect an agent to employee data, I should ask what the worst case is. I haven't asked yet.

beats.trigger: add an agent for a critical dependency, or a plan visualisation.
beats.got: It says to keep working on my real problem, but I'm not sure what a 'critical dependency' is in my case.

take_homes: Start with one agent. Split only when the work needs different access, a different dialect or a different stance. The access test is the one I can use with the works council and the DPO.
Most errors happen at the handoff between agents, and the lesson belongs in a shared rules file so the next person doesn't repeat it. That is how a habit moves from one person to a team.
A combined answer from several agents is not checked for truth. Someone has to own that check, and I can take it to the leadership team.

monday.move: Ask my DPO and the works council contact what is allowed before any employee data goes near an agent. Then draft one single-agent weekly people-metrics summary using only anonymised numbers.
monday.who: Me, my DPO and one HR business partner
monday.when: Ask Monday morning; build the draft later in the week
monday.stop_condition: If the DPO or works council says no or wants a formal process, I stop and wait for the answer.
monday.blocker: Employee data in an AI tool needs the works council and the DPO, and I still haven't asked them.

misconception.why: The module is cautious about agents and says one is often enough. It also says nobody checks whether the output is true, so people still have to review it. That makes me doubt 'agents replace headcount first', but the module never addresses roles or hiring, so I still don't have an answer for the leadership meeting.

one_line: Sensible and honest about when not to use many agents, but it's a tool session, and I'd still need someone to explain what it means for my people.
